defaults.permitted_development: In Wales, a fence, wall or gate is usually permitted development up to 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and up to 2 metres elsewhere, provided no Article 4 direction, planning condition or listed-building curtilage restriction removes that right.

rules.height_rules: The basic Welsh height limits are 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and 2 metres elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate Welsh depth allowance for fences and walls. Height, position and visual impact do the real work in the planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The relationship with the highway boundary is usually the most important siting issue. Front and corner boundaries are far more constrained than enclosed rear-garden positions.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance for a fence, wall or gate. Entrance canopies or other covered features should be assessed separately from the enclosure itself.
rules.materials_rules: Welsh national guidance focuses on height and siting rather than prescribing materials, but visible front boundaries are safest when they use finishes that suit the house and street.

rules.permitted_development: In Wales, a fence, wall or gate is usually permitted development up to 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and up to 2 metres elsewhere, provided no Article 4 direction, planning condition or listed-building curtilage restriction removes that right.

rules.height_rules: Most Welsh fence and wall cases are decided by the familiar split between the 1 metre highway-edge limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Thickness is rarely the deciding point for a Welsh fence or wall; the questions are usually height, highway relationship and heritage sensitivity.
rules.boundary_rules: A fence or wall can be acceptable on one boundary and not on another. Welsh highway-facing positions usually receive the closest planning attention because of visibility and street character.

rules.materials_rules: There is no fixed Welsh material list for fences and walls, yet heritage-sensitive areas often expect a boundary treatment that looks restrained and appropriate to the setting.

restrictions.conservation_area: Boundary works in a conservation area are more sensitive, and an Article 4 direction can remove ordinary permitted development rights.
restrictions.listed_building: You need planning permission for boundary works to a listed house or within the curtilage of a listed building, and listed building consent may also be required.
